title: Commodity stocks: how the materials cycle works
description: Commodity stocks are priced by the commodity, not the brand. The four families, the cycle's margin leverage and the sector's medians against the market.
author: AK1A Research Lab
body:
Commodity stocks are the companies that take the world out of the ground, the forest and the air — mines, steel mills, sawmills and fertilizer plants — and pass it on at a price set on the commodity exchange, not by the company itself. That one property explains almost everything else in the sector's market data: margins swing with the cycle, not marketing budgets. In AK1A's company universe — 100 companies, ten per sector, key ratios fetched 2026-09-03 from Yahoo Finance and MarketStack — the materials sector's median trades at 1.3 times book value, against 2.7 for the whole market. The operating margin sits at 9.7 percent against 21.2. Roughly half the valuation and half the margin: the commodity cycle imprinted in two key ratios.

This guide walks the four families, the margin lever's mechanics, the two classic traps in reading key ratios — and three checks that hold when you read a commodity stock. So the method works, from the ground up.

## What commodity stocks are — four families

The materials sector gathers companies that extract or process raw materials. The universe's ten Swedish and Nordic companies — Boliden, Newmont, SSAB, Norsk Hydro, SCA, Holmen, Billerud, Stora Enso, UPM and Yara — divide naturally into four families:

- **Metals and mining.** Boliden (zinc, copper, precious metals) and Newmont (gold). The margin is driven by the metal price against the cost per tonne of ore.
- **Steel and aluminium.** SSAB and Norsk Hydro. Smelters and mills with high fixed costs; prices are set globally, swinging with construction and manufacturing.
- **Forest, paper and packaging.** SCA, Holmen, Billerud, Stora Enso and UPM — from timber to pulp, carton and paper, often with energy and forest land as a second leg.
- **Fertilizers.** Yara: ammonia and fertilizer, where end demand is world food production.

Common to all four: the product is interchangeable with the competitor's. The customer chooses on price and specification — not on brand. The difference from a brand-based business, where the pricing sits in the product, explains why the sector's [sector medians](/blogg/branschmedianer-akm2) look as they do.

## A price set on the world market — the price-taker's mechanics

A commodity company is a price taker: the product's price is given by the world market, and the company's whole room for maneuver lies on the cost side — break-even cost, energy, currencies and scale. Combine that with high fixed costs (a mine or paper machine costs as much to run in a boom as in a slump) and you get the margin lever: when the commodity price rises, the increase falls almost straight through to earnings; when it falls, the same mechanics cut in reverse.

A single year's margin thus says more about where in the cycle the company sat than about how it is run. This is the difference from [revenue diversification](/blogg/intaktsdiversifiering-risken-som-inte-syns-i-pe) in other sectors: even a broad customer base helps little when all of demand — construction, cars, packaging, farming — turns at once.

## Commodity stocks in numbers — the medians against the market

This is the sector's median against the whole universe (100 companies, data fetched 2026-09-03; sources Yahoo Finance and MarketStack):

- **P/B:** 1.3 against 2.7 — half the market's book-value multiple.
- **P/E:** 18.5 against 20.4 — the gap is smaller than it looks; more shortly.
- **EV/EBIT:** 17.7 against 19.5.
- **Operating margin:** 9.7 percent against 21.2 — gross margin 33.5 against 47.8.
- **ROE:** 7.2 percent against 14.9.
- **Revenue growth five years:** −2.2 percent a year against +3.5 for the market.

Three observations from the rows. First: the low P/B reflects a capital-intensive business — mines, blast furnaces and forest land tie up capital that cannot be turned over quickly, and the market prices it low in the lower part of the cycle. In fact, four of the ten — the entire forest group of Billerud, Stora Enso, SCA and Holmen — traded below book value. Second: an ROE of 7.2 percent is not a sign of badly run companies but of margins in the cycle's weak part during the measurement period. Third: the negative five-year revenue growth is the commodity price's own doing — in volumes (tonnes, cubic meters) many companies grew, but prices per unit fell. Revenue in a commodity report is price times volume, and the company does not own the former.

## The cycle's two traps: P/E and the single-year snapshot

The first trap is the P/E ratio read without the cycle. Earnings — the E — are at their highest just as the cycle turns down, which gives low multiples at the top and high at the bottom, the reverse of a structurally growing sector's multiple. The universe illustrates the pattern: Yara posted the lowest P/E of the ten (8.3) while consensus earnings growth was negative (−21 percent) — the classic combination of peak earnings and falling expectations. One company, Billerud, lacks a P/E: last year's margin was negative, and dividing by a negative E gives no meaningful multiple. When the multiple disappears, it is not the data missing — it is the key ratio itself that stops working. Rule: in cyclicals, compare multiples against the company's own history through a full cycle, never a universal average. The deep dive: the course [P/E — a deep dive](/kurser/km-009-pe).

The second trap is the single-year snapshot — reading one year as the state of things. The control is rolling several years: the median margin through a full cycle — the "mid-cycle margin" — is the commodity company's normal state. In valuation terms the same logic makes [the P/B ratio](/blogg/pb-tal-nar-jamfor-man-bokvarde-ratt) and [EV/EBITDA](/blogg/sa-raknar-du-ev-ebitda) more useful than P/E here, pricing capital and cash flow rather than a single year's earnings. In the course [relative valuation](/kurser/km-011-relativ-vardering) the method is built step by step.

## Three checks when you read a commodity company

- **Check 1 — the margin against its own history.** Calculate the operating margin five to ten years back and note where today sits against its median. That is the cycle measurement; a margin 40 percent above its own historical median has more often been a peak than a new normal.
- **Check 2 — the balance sheet through the cycle.** Because peak earnings tempt toward peak investment, net debt against [EBITDA through the cycle](/kurser/km-010-evebit) — not just the peak year's — is the reading that matters; [the debt-to-equity ratio's levels](/blogg/skuldsattningsgrad-vilken-niva-ar-farlig) walks through the boundaries.
- **Check 3 — what the price presupposes.** Set today's multiple against mid-cycle earnings: does the multiplied normal earnings land above, below or at today's price? That is the core of [scenario analysis](/kurser/km-029-scenarioanalys) and handling [the margin of safety](/kurser/km-030-margin-of-safety) in a sector where next year rarely resembles the last.

## The families differ — and it shows in the data

The cycle is shared, but the drivers differ: gold has no industrial demand cycle but is driven by real interest rates and central banks; steel swings with construction and manufacturing; the forest companies have seen demand shift from graphic paper toward packaging and energy; fertilizer follows farming and the European gas price. The differences are the argument behind [sum-of-the-parts analysis](/kurser/km-012-sum-of-the-parts-sotp) — several of the forest companies are in practice several businesses (forest land, pulp, energy, packaging) under one listing. In a portfolio, commodity companies are assets whose co-movement with other stocks is not constant — [the basics of correlation](/kurser/km-014-korrelation-diversifiering) explains why that matters to total risk. The sector's whole methodology is gathered in the course [the materials sector](/kurser/km-045-materialsektorn).

## The summary

- Commodity companies are price takers: the product is priced on the world market, the whole room for maneuver lies on the cost side — and the margin lever makes earnings cycle-shaped.
- The median: P/B 1.3 against the market's 2.7, operating margin 9.7 against 21.2 percent, ROE 7.2 against 14.9 (universe 100 companies, 2026-09-03).
- P/E fails at cycle tops — Yara's 8.3 with a negative earnings forecast and Billerud's missing P/E show the pattern in actual data.
- Three checks: margin against own history, balance sheet through the cycle, price against normal-year earnings.

The continuation track: [the materials sector](/kurser/km-045-materialsektorn) covers the sector's analysis tools, and [the complete guide to Swedish stock analysis](/blogg/komplett-guide-svensk-aktieanalys-2026) places the sector in the whole.

_Data sources: AK1A's company universe (100 companies; Yahoo Finance and MarketStack, fetched 2026-09-03). Key ratios per latest financial year and latest price._
